Gastroenterology · published research

Microbiota

PBM has altered microbiome measures in small human cohorts and animal models, but findings vary by site and protocol. The evidence does not establish that these shifts cause a clinical benefit.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

PBM has altered microbiome measures in small human cohorts and animal models, but findings vary by site and protocol. The evidence does not establish that these shifts cause a clinical benefit.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact “Microbiome” subcategory contains ten records: six reviews and four empirical publications, including three small human reports and one mouse study. Broader PBM records also examine microbial outcomes under indications such as Parkinson’s disease, colitis, diabetes, stress, and oral mucositis. Those additional reports cannot be combined into a single count of independent microbiome trials: the 2022 Parkinson paper reanalysed samples from a previously published 12-person treatment cohort, and a 2026 five-year Parkinson follow-up reused six members of an earlier PBM proof-of-concept cohort. That is overlapping follow-up, not an independent treatment cohort. Reviews also repeat findings from primary studies.

Human and clinical evidence

The 2022 Parkinson microbiome analysis reported post-treatment shifts in stool composition and a change in the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio after a 12-week abdominal, neck, head, and nose PBM programme. It explicitly analysed samples from an earlier clinical study, so it adds a microbiome outcome, not a new treatment cohort (Bicknell et al. 2022). A separate breast-cancer case report sampled one person before and after radiotherapy/immunotherapy and PBM. Some microbial taxa and diversity measures changed after treatment, but a single timeline cannot separate light effects from other treatment or time effects (Bicknell et al. 2022).

A four-person oral-mucositis pilot reported fewer selected pathogenic oral species and more commensal bacteria alongside changes in inflammatory markers. A later six-person randomized split-mouth study in periodontal-orthodontic patients found no significant change in overall plaque microbial community structure or periodontal measures. These are oral-site results and do not establish change in the gut microbiome (Zanotta et al. 2020; Zhang et al. 2026).

A 2026 five-year case series analysed stool samples from six Parkinson participants who had continued the earlier PBM programme. The report found reduced microbial evenness and altered taxonomic composition over time. The authors note that the small uncontrolled series cannot separate PBM from diet, lifestyle, or other time-related influences; its participants also came from the earlier treatment cohort (Bicknell et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

In mice, abdominal near-infrared treatment changed microbial diversity and increased Allobaculum after repeated 808-nm exposures, while a single red-light treatment did not produce the same result. Other animal studies report shifts in gut microbes alongside changes in inflammation, metabolism, or behavior. These findings show that treatment timing and the model affect which microbial measures change, but they do not establish that a particular shift is beneficial or directly causes an organism-level outcome (Bicknell et al. 2019).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No substantial independent in-vitro evidence was identified. One animal-linked programme also tested cultured gut organisms ex vivo; those assays were part of the same research line.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols include 660-nm red visible and 808-nm near-infrared abdominal laser treatment in mice, 904-nm near-infrared abdominal treatment in a human case, 970-nm near-infrared intraoral treatment for oral mucositis, and 940-nm near-infrared monthly intraoral irradiation during six-month orthodontic retention. Targets, doses, timing, microbial sampling, and sequencing methods differ. No head-to-head study establishes an optimal wavelength or schedule, and oral, gut, and skin microbiomes should not be treated as interchangeable.

Interpretation

The reports show that PBM can coincide with measurable microbiome shifts in some settings, while other studies find no overall community change. The direction and meaning depend on the taxa, body site, and outcome examined. Current evidence does not show that a microbiome shift itself caused an improvement in disease or patient health.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term microbiome composition changes in small human cohorts Very low for clinical benefit caused by microbiome changes
Publications and records25 relevant articles (two non-PBM candidates excluded)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Small human reports and several animal models show that microbiome measures can change after PBM, but results vary by body site, treatment, and organism. One Parkinson microbiome paper reanalysed samples from an earlier clinical cohort, so it is not an independent treatment trial. Controlled studies linking reproducible functional microbiome changes to patient outcomes are needed for a stronger conclusion.
